meta.backstory:
Being blocked used to be an experience engineers sat inside. You noticed progress had stalled, isolated why, and — the hard part — put it into words precise enough that a teammate could act on them. That articulation was the skill: "we're blocked on X because Y" is how engineers escalate, how teams route work, how organizations learn where the friction lives.

Coding agents remove the sitting-inside. When progress stalls, the reflex is no longer to diagnose but to re-prompt: rephrase the request, paste more context, try another model. The blocker is never named because it never has to be — the agent either gets past it or the attempt is abandoned. The pain that trained the skill is gone, and so, gradually, is the skill.

The cost shows up in communication before it shows up in code. Status updates degrade from "blocked on the auth service's rate limits" to "the agent isn't getting it." Escalations arrive without a nameable cause. The engineers most fluent with agents can be the least able to say what, precisely, is standing in their way — and an engineer who can't name what stops them can't ask for the right help.
